answer_text:
# 💙 A History of Blue: The World's Most Elusive Colour

---

## I. The Colour That Had No Name

Of all the colours that have shaped human history, none has a story quite as strange, as expensive, or as triumphant as blue. Its journey is almost implausible: a colour that dominates our sky and seas, and yet for much of human history, it was barely acknowledged — and barely achievable.

Due to blue's rarity in nature, it has a shorter history than other colours. Blue is not present in cave paintings from 20,000 years ago, and the Ancient Greeks did not even have a term for it. While red and black ochres were smeared across prehistoric cave walls with ease, blue simply did not exist as a workable pigment in the ancient world. Linguistic research confirms that languages do not begin by having a word for blue. Colour names typically began with black and white, then red — and blue was added last, probably only once blue pigments could be manufactured reliably in a given culture.

The Greeks and Romans didn't have a word for the colour blue. For Homer, the sea was "wine-red." Blue was associated with the barbaric Celts who supposedly dyed their bodies blue for battle, and women with blue eyes were thought to have loose morals. In ancient Rome, blue was the colour of the barbarians, the foreigners. There wasn't even a native name for it — the word had to be borrowed from the Germanic *blau* or the Arabic *azraq*.

---

## II. Egypt's Great Invention

While the Greeks looked the other way, the Egyptians looked at their beloved lapis lazuli and turquoise stones and decided: *we must have this colour.* The Egyptians loved lapis and turquoise so much that they invented the first synthetic blue pigment in order to affordably copy their unique colour. "Egyptian blue" was made by mixing silica, lime, copper, and alkali, and it could be used on stone, wood, plaster, papyrus and canvas. The many decorative objects that have survived attest to the presence of blue in Egyptian life.

The Ancient Egyptians created the first blue pigment around 2,200 B.C., by heating a mixture of sand, ground limestone, and copper-containing minerals like malachite or azurite at a high temperature. Scholars argue that for many millennia, civilisations prized the rare stone, believing it to have mystical properties. Lapis lazuli was particularly popular in ancient Sumer and ancient Egypt, where it was used for jewellery, headdresses, and even the tomb of Tutankhamun, as well as the eyeshadow of Cleopatra.

---

## III. The Price of Blue: Ultramarine

For Renaissance Europe, blue was not simply a colour — it was a currency. Painters had to grind up the semi-precious stone lapis lazuli to make ultramarine, the deep blue pigment that is the hallmark of many Renaissance paintings. The name comes from the Latin *ultramarinus*, meaning "beyond the sea," because the stones were imported from mines in Afghanistan by Italian traders in the 14th and 15th centuries.

This pigment was regularly imported from Asia, across the Silk Road, dating back 6,000 years until the eighteenth century. Extracted from the remote Sar-e-Sang valley in the Badakhshan mountains of Afghanistan, it would eventually make its way to the bustling cosmopolitan towns of western Europe.

Ultramarine was once so expensive it cost more than gold. Ultramarine was so expensive that some paintings were never finished because the painter couldn't afford to buy more pigment. Even Michelangelo couldn't afford it, and Raphael used it only for a top coat.

---

## IV. The Virgin's Robe

It was the Catholic Church that transformed blue from a barbarian's colour into a divine one. In the twelfth century, the Catholic Church dictated to Rome and the rest of Europe that painters depict the Virgin Mary in the most expensive colour — blue. Because of its cost, blue was reserved only for the most important subjects. In the Renaissance, nobody was more important than the Virgin Mary. Because she was almost always painted wearing blue, the colour became synonymous with purity, humility, and the divine.

In Christian iconography, blue became one of the most sacred colours. The religious connotations of the pigment were also because it was so expensive — artists preserved the most costly colours for important religious subject matters, like the Virgin Mary. A particular shade was even named after her: "Marian blue."

As people began to associate blue with the Virgin Mary, the colour became a powerful element in church decoration and symbolism. Blue gained new favour as a royal colour in the twelfth century and became a formidable political and military force during the French Revolution.

---

## V. Making Blue Affordable: Prussian Blue & Synthetic Ultramarine

The age of blue's exclusivity could not last forever. The invention of Prussian blue in 1720 popularised darker tones that were quickly adopted by Romantic painters and poets.

Then came a race to democratise the colour completely. In 1824, the Société d'Encouragement offered a reward to whoever could invent a synthetic blue. German professor Christian Gmelin competed with French chemist Jean-Baptiste Guimet, and after some contention, the award was given to Guimet. It was consequently named French Ultramarine.

Once blue became affordable and available, its usages soared. Thanks to the Impressionist movement, blue became the atmospheric colour of choice, no longer reserved only for the raiment of the Virgin Mary.

---

## VI. Blue for the Workers — and the World

With blue now accessible, it found its way off church walls and into everyday life. Jean fabric was first produced in Genoa, Italy in the 17th century; the French city of Nîmes copied the technique shortly after ('de Nîmes'... aka 'denim'). The cotton twill fabric, dyed with indigo, was sturdy and washable, making it perfect for workers. Levi Strauss kicked the fabric up a notch when he patented the use of metal rivets to reinforce the seams on denim pants in 1873.

In the 19th century, synthetic blue dyes and pigments gradually replaced organic dyes and mineral pigments. Dark blue became a common colour for military uniforms and, later, in the late 20th century, for business suits.

---

## VII. Klein Blue & the Digital Age

In the 20th century, one artist declared war on the world's definition of blue. Between 1947 and 1957, the French artist Yves Klein perfected what he considered the purest blue of all. He registered International Klein Blue (IKB) as a trademark, and the deep ultramarine became his signature. He painted over 200 canvases with the colour, as well as many sculptures, and even painted models in IKB so they could "print" their bodies onto canvas.

Then came the Internet.
